title: Adivasi Filmmaker Ravi Raj Murmu Wins National Award for Self-Made Santhali Short Film
excerpt: The 33-year-old FTII graduate from Jharkhand directed, shot, edited, and produced his 12-minute debut 'Angen' after failing to find backers for a Santhali-language project.
body:
• Ravi Raj Murmu, a 33-year-old Adivasi filmmaker from Jharkhand, won the Golden Lotus (Swarna Kamal) for Best Debut Film of a Director in the non-feature category at the 72nd National Film Awards.
  • His 12-minute Santhali-language short film 'Angen' (Invisible) was entirely self-produced — Murmu served as director, writer, cinematographer, editor, production designer, and producer after failing to secure external funding.
  • A graduate of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII) in Pune, Murmu previously worked as an associate editor on mainstream Bollywood productions including Good Luck Jerry.
  • The award marks a rare national spotlight on Santhali cinema, a micro-industry that typically operates on budgets under ₹25 lakh with minimal distribution infrastructure.

A One-Man Film Crew

When the 72nd National Film Awards were announced on July 18, one name stood out in the non-feature film section: Ravi Raj Murmu, a 33-year-old Santal filmmaker from Jharkhand who had never directed a film before. His 12-minute short, Angen — Santhali for "Invisible" — won the Golden Lotus (Swarna Kamal) for Best Debut Film of a Director, carrying a cash prize of ₹3 lakh, according to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

What made the win remarkable was how the film was made. Unable to find anyone willing to fund a short film in Santhali — a language spoken by roughly 7.6 million people, mostly across Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar — Murmu did virtually everything himself. His IMDb credits for Angen list him as director, writer, cinematographer, editor, production designer, executive producer, and producer.

"Every story I write comes from Jharkhand. They're rooted in Adivasi life."

— Ravi Raj Murmu, director of Angen

From FTII to Bollywood's Back Rooms

Murmu's path to the National Award ran through India's premier film school. He enrolled at the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII) in Pune in 2016, completing a postgraduate diploma in film editing in 2019. The institute, which has produced directors like Adoor Gopalakrishnan and Mani Kaul, gave Murmu technical fluency — but not an easy route to making films in his own language.

After graduating, Murmu found work in the Hindi film industry, serving as an associate editor on the 2022 comedy Good Luck Jerry and as editor and associate director on Burbokor Khel – Game of Fools the same year. In 2023, he worked as cinematographer on the short film Man, Melody & Dolls. Each role sharpened a different skill — editing, camera work, directing — that he would eventually deploy single-handedly on Angen.

Santhali Cinema's Chronic Funding Gap

Murmu's struggle to find financial backing is not unique. Santhali cinema operates on the margins of India's film industry, with budgets typically ranging from ₹15 lakh to ₹25 lakh for full-length feature films, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. The first Santhali feature film, Chando Lekhan, was produced only in 2000 by actor-turned-filmmaker Dashrath Hansda, who had to personally hire theatres to prove the commercial viability of films in the language.

Two decades later, the infrastructure remains sparse. Distribution networks are limited, funding sources are scarce, and the audience, while loyal, is geographically dispersed. Tribal filmmakers in Jharkhand have long spoken about resorting to crowdfunding, personal savings, or convincing villagers to act for free to get their projects off the ground.

The 72nd National Film Awards received 161 entries in the non-feature category alone. That Murmu's self-funded, self-shot debut rose above the competition speaks both to his technical skill and to the jury's willingness to recognize cinema from India's linguistic margins.

A Broader Shift at the National Awards

Murmu's win fits a wider pattern at the 72nd National Film Awards, which honoured films in an unusually diverse array of languages. The feature film section recognized titles in Santhali's constitutional sibling languages — Best Assamese Film went to Juiphool, Best Odia Film to Lahari, Best Manipuri Film to Sunita — alongside commercial blockbusters like Kalki 2898 AD (Best Popular Film) and Article 370 (Best Feature Film). Best Garhwali Film and Best Tulu Film awards were also handed out.

The non-feature section, chaired by Aseem Sinha, similarly leaned toward independent and regional work. The Best Non-Feature Film went to Bhangaar, a Marathi-English production by Sumira Roy, while Bollywood director Aanand L. Rai won Best Direction for Statue of Unity – Ekta ka Prateek.

What Comes Next

For India's roughly 12 million Adivasi people who identify with Santhali language and culture, Murmu's Golden Lotus is a landmark. The award ceremony, to be held at Vigyan Bhawan in New Delhi with awards presented by the President of India, will put Murmu on the same stage as winners from India's largest film industries.

Whether the recognition translates into funding for his next project — or for Santhali cinema more broadly — remains an open question. India's National Film Awards can launch careers, but the structural barriers facing indigenous-language filmmakers extend well beyond a single prize. For now, Murmu has proved that a 12-minute film in a language most Indians have never heard can hold its own against the country's best.
